analysis.one_liner: Bars the federal government from buying food from contractors paying below local prevailing wages.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and a subcommittee and never received a hearing, a vote, or further action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop the Department of Agriculture from buying meat, poultry, or processed food from any company whose U.S. workers are paid below the prevailing local wage and benefits rate for that kind of work. The Labor Department would set those rates, taking union contracts into account, and no rate could undercut an existing union agreement. It would apply only to companies in the federal food supply chain, not the whole meat industry.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at meatpacking and processed-food companies that sell to the federal government, who could see pay and benefits lifted to the prevailing local rate for their jobs. Union contracts would be explicitly protected.

how_it_helps.text: Companies selling meat, poultry, or processed food to the Department of Agriculture could not pay their U.S. workers below the prevailing local wage and fringe benefit rate for that work [S2][S3].

The Labor Department would set the prevailing rates and must take existing local collective bargaining agreements into account, so union standards would anchor the floor rather than be undercut [S2][S3].
Nothing in the bill could supersede wages and benefits already negotiated in a union contract, protecting existing agreements from being dragged down [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Meat and processed-food companies that sell to the federal government and currently pay below the local prevailing rate would bear higher labor costs, some of which could be passed into the prices the government pays for food.

drawbacks.text: The bill would apply only to the federal supply chain, so the majority of meat and poultry workers outside it would see no direct benefit [S2][S3].

Contractors facing higher labor costs could pass them into their bids, modestly raising what the government — and ultimately taxpayers — pays for food it buys for programs like school lunches and military feeding [S3].
Requiring the Labor Department to determine prevailing rates by locality for food-processing jobs would add compliance and administrative costs for contractors and federal agencies [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but narrow: it would raise pay for a slice of the meatpacking workforce — an industry known for low wages and hazardous work — without touching non-federal employers. The cost is higher contract prices where wages rise, and the design is defensible since it protects existing union contracts. Its main weakness is scope, not design.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Agriculture Committee, was passed down to a subcommittee, and never got a hearing or a vote before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Pocan introduced the bill on July 11, 2023, joined by Rep. Greg Casar [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee the same day and never received floor action [S5].
On August 24, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry, where it remained [S5].
The bill had only one cosponsor and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with no hearing, markup, or vote ever scheduled [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Contractors in the federal meat and processed-food supply chain keep paying whatever wages they choose, since no purchasing condition was ever imposed; the workers the bill aimed to help gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal food contractors and their suppliers

for.name: Rep. Mark Pocan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require prevailing wages for workers at companies selling food to the federal government.

for.name: Rep. Greg Casar
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor of the bill, introduced alongside Pocan.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Glenn Thompson, R-WI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill in July 2023, referred it to the Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry Subcommittee in August 2023, and never held a hearing or markup before Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, and no Republican supported it; the bill never advanced far enough for a floor vote to show the full party split.

industries.industry: Meat and poultry processors selling to the federal government
industries.note: These companies would have had to pay at least the prevailing local wage and benefits rate to keep selling meat and poultry to the Department of Agriculture, raising costs for any that pay below it. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against the pay of the workers processing their products.

The same prevailing-wage condition would extend to processed food sold to the federal government, covering a broader set of food contractors. Workers below the local prevailing rate would be entitled to more pay.

industries.industry: Federal food procurement and institutional food buyers
industries.note: Programs that buy food with federal dollars — school meals, military feeding — could face somewhat higher contract prices if contractors pass wage costs through. In exchange, the federal government's purchasing power would be used to raise pay in its supply chain.
